headline: Alberta's AI Data Centre Bet Meets Reality: The Public
subheadline: Government all-in on tech infrastructure play; 42% of voters want pause to actually understand what they're paying for.
source_headline: Alberta is all in on AI data centres. A new poll suggests the public isn't
body_html:
Alberta's government has apparently decided that the province's economic future hinges on becoming North America's premium real estate agent for artificial intelligence compute. The strategy is straightforward: position Alberta as a jurisdiction that will rubber-stamp approvals for massive data centre operations at the speed of venture capital impatience, then watch the billions roll in. But a new Leger survey has introduced an inconvenient variable into this beautifully simple equation: actual Albertans, who have started asking questions that governments typically prefer people don't ask until after the ribbon-cutting ceremonies.

According to the poll, 42 per cent of respondents want a temporary pause on new data centre approvals until an independent public review examines the effects on—well, the survey cuts off mid-sentence, which is perhaps fitting. The effects on electricity? Water? Air quality? The provincial budget? The jobs situation for non-tech workers? Whatever it was going to say, clearly felt important enough that nearly half the electorate wanted someone to figure it out before signing away more Crown land and utility capacity. This is what happens when you let people read the fine print before committing to infrastructure megadeals: they develop concerns, ask for evidence, request transparency—all deeply inconvenient obstacles to moving fast and breaking things, or in Alberta's case, moving fast and breaking grid capacity.

The truly satirical part isn't that Alberta is pursuing data centre development—that's rational industrial policy. It's that the government has apparently been operating under the assumption that major infrastructure commitments affecting electricity consumption, environmental footprint, and long-term resource allocation simply don't require public buy-in until after the deal is done. A 42 per cent "pause first, approve later" response isn't overwhelming skepticism; it's a relatively polite way of saying "we have questions you haven't answered." In VC-speak, this would be called "founder-market fit risk." In democratic terms, it's voters noting that their elected officials seem more excited about tech sector enthusiasm than about, say, basic due diligence.

The government's pitch, presumably, centres on job creation, economic diversification, and positioning Alberta as a global AI infrastructure hub—all perfectly defensible arguments presented with maximum enthusiasm and minimum specificity. Data centres will require electricity (lots), cooling (lots), and will generate revenue (eventually, maybe). What they'll require from existing residents in terms of grid reliability, environmental trade-offs, and opportunity costs remains conveniently unexamined. This is the founder's dilemma applied to provincial policy: the vision is compelling, the upside narrative is intoxicating, and the independent review of downside risks keeps getting scheduled for next quarter.

What makes this story a perfect microcosm of contemporary deal-making is that nobody in this scenario is unreasonable. Alberta wants economic growth. Data centre operators want favorable regulatory conditions. The public wants to understand what they're trading in return. These positions are fundamentally compatible, yet they're being treated as mutually exclusive. A temporary pause for independent review isn't a rejection of the data centre strategy—it's a request for honesty about its actual implications. That this request is polling at 42 per cent suggests that roughly two in five Albertans have already figured out what deal-makers everywhere prefer to keep obscured: that enthusiasm and evidence are different things.

When the poll also reveals that Albertans "aren't overwhelmingly skeptical,
saying: We're willing to listen, but you're going to have to show your work." Good luck running a tech-forward economic strategy on the basis of transparency and accountability. That's not disruption; that's just accountability, which is apparently the scariest four-letter word in modern industrial policy.
glossary_definition: A process by which citizens request evidence for major decisions before they're already implemented.
